strengths: Well-motivated problem: clearly identifies why existing online curation methods fail for detection (unstable loss signals, architectural complexity), addressing an underexplored gap
Principled metric-aligned approach: anchors sample selection to dataset-level mAP rather than loss values, avoiding architecture-specific instabilities
Efficient closed-form computation: derives O(1) analytic solutions (Eq. 10) with Monte Carlo verification (Figure 5), enabling practical online scoring

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: 6 diverse detector architectures with consistent ~2.0 mAP improvements, thorough ablations, noise robustness testing (up to +6.9 mAP at 100% noise), and detailed comparisons (Table 5)
Practical architecture-agnosticism: operates only on forward outputs without modifying detector code, loss functions, or schedules; easy plug-and-play integration
Thoughtful design addressing overfitting: recognizes that pure online sampling collapses to narrow subspace and combines with strong augmentation to maintain diversity (Table 2)
Convergence acceleration: achieves baseline performance in 52% fewer iterations (Figure 7) and maintains performance under varying noise conditions
Extensive supplementary material: rigorous mathematical derivations, implementation pseudocode, Monte Carlo verification, and detailed ablations strengthen reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: teacher-student learnability (RHO-LOSS, JEST, ACED) and AP-based selection ([61]) are established; main contribution is their combination for detection with closed-form computation, which is somewhat incremental

Uniform distribution assumption lacks rigorous justification: posed only as 'maximum entropy baseline' without explaining why real TP/FP score distributions (which follow Beta distributions per Appendix 6) perform identically on validation; model-specific priors achieve nearly identical val AP (Table 11) undermining the theoretical foundation

Substantial training overhead inadequately addressed: 2.5× wall-clock training time is significant; framed as 'offline investment' but no cost-benefit analysis vs. alternatives or comparison of wall-clock-time-normalized improvements with other methods

Strong teacher dependency contradicts model-agnostic claim: requires pretrained teacher; Appendix 1 shows cross-architecture teachers degrade performance (e.g., Swin/DETR→R-CNN yields 38.6 vs 39.9 mAP); adds compute cost and architectural coupling

Tight coupling to data augmentation design: online sampling alone causes severe overfitting (Table 2: +5.7 train, -0.1 val); method requires detector-specific augmentation (Table 10) with 'relatively naïve' scheme, making gains partially attributable to augmentation rather than sampling logic

Limited evaluation scope: only COCO 2017 with ResNet backbones; no evaluation on other datasets (Pascal VOC, CityScapes, BDD100K) or diverse backbones (Vision Transformers, modern CNNs), limiting generalizability claims

Modest empirical improvements given computational cost: ~2.0 mAP average gain (range 1.6–3.0) with 2.5× training overhead yields unfavorable cost-benefit; no confidence intervals/multiple runs make statistical significance unclear; image-wise AP baseline [61] difference is only 1.7 mAP (38.3→40.0 for Faster R-CNN)

Insufficient analysis of sample selection patterns: no systematic analysis of which samples DetGain prioritizes (hard negatives, scales, rare classes); Figure 1 provides only anecdotal examples; no per-class AP breakdown to assess long-tail class handling despite claims of natural mitigation

Additive approximation validity not empirically validated: assumes δmAP(B) ≈ Σ δmAP(x) with b ≪ D; with k=20% sampling, O(|B|/|D|) error may not be negligible on COCO (118k images), yet error is not quantified

Knowledge distillation relationship unclear: Table 6 shows DetGain alone achieves similar gains as single-teacher KD (+2.3 vs +2.4 mAP); unclear if DetGain is selecting samples favorable to KD by design or complementary; combined gain (+3.7 mAP) may reflect additive effects rather than synergy

Statistical rigor absent: all results are single runs without error bars, confidence intervals, or multiple seeds; impossible to assess variance or significance for ~2.0 mAP improvements within typical benchmark noise

Missing practical guidance: no analysis of failure modes, performance on extreme long-tail distributions, sensitivity to hyperparameters (super-batch size, augmentation strength), or when 2.5× overhead is justified relative to gains

strengths: Well-motivated problem identification with clear diagnosis of why loss-based curation fails for object detection (fragmented losses, stochastic assignment, complex per-image definitions)
Rigorous mathematical framework with correct Stieltjes integral formulation and verified closed-form solutions (Figure 5 Monte Carlo validation shows excellent agreement)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across six diverse detectors with consistent ~2.0 mAP improvements and extensive ablations on key components
Architecture-agnostic design operating at data-pipeline level using only standard detection outputs, enabling applicability across codebases and detector families
Thorough robustness validation under annotation noise, pseudo-labels, and complementarity analysis with knowledge distillation methods
weaknesses: Incremental novelty: core idea of teacher-student gap for sample selection extends directly from RHO-LOSS/JEST/ACED; main contribution is adapting via AP-based scoring rather than introducing new principles

Significant practical overhead: 2.5× wall-clock training time for ~2.0 mAP gains (≈0.8 mAP per 1.5× slowdown); paper downplays this as 'offline investment' but practitioners need total training time analysis

Strong data augmentation dependency contradicts simplicity claims: sampling alone causes overfitting (-0.1 mAP, Table 2); requires detector-family-specific augmentation hyperparameters (Table 10), undermining 'architecture-agnostic' framing

Uniform Beta(1,1) prior assumption lacks rigorous validation: while computationally justified, model-specific priors show negligible improvement only on COCO; generalization to other datasets/score distributions untested
Additive batch approximation δmAP(B)≈Σδ(x) undervalidated: assumed accurate when b≪D but no empirical study of approximation error; critical assumption deserves ablation across batch sizes

Teacher-student architecture matching requirement limits practicality: Table 7 shows asynchronous architectures yield significant drops; requirement for same-family teacher adds overhead vs. claims of minimally intrusive integration
Missing sample-level analysis: no visualization of which image types DetGain prioritizes; lacks interpretation of what makes samples 'informative' or analysis of failure cases

Single-benchmark evaluation: all experiments on COCO 2017 only; generalization to other domains (Pascal VOC, custom datasets, different scales) unclear; cross-dataset validation would strengthen claims
Statistical rigor absent: no confidence intervals, error bars, or multiple-run reporting; improvements could be within noise for some detector-schedule combinations

Incomplete baseline comparisons: Image-AP method [61] achieves 38.3-40.0 AP vs. DetGain 40.0-41.6—margin not overwhelming given added complexity; missing comparisons with curriculum learning and recent active learning methods

strengths: Well-motivated problem: Clearly identifies why loss-based learnability fails for detection (fragmented losses, stochastic sampling, architecture complexity) and proposes principled metric-aware alternative using AP instead of loss

Sound mathematical framework: Rigorous Stieltjes integral formulation (Eq. 6), correct derivation of marginal TP/FP contributions (Eqs. 7-8), and closed-form O(1) solutions under uniform prior verified by Monte Carlo simulation (Figure 5)

Comprehensive experimental validation: Consistent improvements (~1.6-3.0 mAP) across 6 diverse detector families (Faster R-CNN, ATSS, FCOS, GFL, VFNet, Deformable DETR); outperforms loss-based, gradient-based, entropy-based, and image-AP baselines in fair comparisons (Table 5)

Strong robustness analysis: Controlled annotation noise experiments up to 100% (Figure 4), pseudo-label scenarios (Table 8), and synthetic corruption types demonstrate stability vs. loss-based methods

Practical design: Architecture-agnostic (works post-hoc with standard detector outputs), minimally intrusive (data pipeline only), compatible with knowledge distillation using single teacher (Table 6)

Thorough ablation studies: Quantifies necessity of both augmentation and sampling (Table 2), teacher capacity effects (Table 3), sampling ratio trade-offs (Table 4), and alternative prior assumptions (Table 11 and Appendix 6)

Excellent reproducibility: Provides detailed algorithms, pseudocode (Listing 1), implementation details, augmentation specifications, hyperparameters, and Monte Carlo verification strengthening confidence in technical correctness
weaknesses: Significant training computational overhead of ~2.5× wall-clock time (Table 4) makes experimentation expensive; while inference cost is unaffected, development cycle overhead could be prohibitive in resource-constrained settings

Practical teacher dependency: Requires pretrained teacher on same training set; Appendix 1 shows architectural mismatch severely hurts performance (e.g., SwinL teacher with Faster R-CNN student: 38.6 mAP vs. 39.9 with ResNet-101), creating circular dependency where practitioners must first train a good detector

Uniform prior approximation is crude despite computational efficiency; Table 11 shows detector-specific Beta prior yields comparable validation performance but higher training AP, and justification relies on ranking being more important than absolute values—incomplete empirical validation

Limited experimental scope: Evaluation restricted to COCO 2017 only with no results on other detection benchmarks (Pascal VOC, Objects365, Cityscapes) to demonstrate generalization across domains and datasets

Data augmentation coupling confounds attribution: Method requires strong online augmentation to prevent overfitting (Table 2); augmentation details scattered in appendix with detector-specific tuning (Table 10) makes it difficult to isolate DetGain's independent contribution

Insufficient sample selection analysis: No visualization of selected vs. rejected samples, DetGain score distributions, or what patterns characterize 'informative' samples; missing error analysis of when/why method fails

First-order additive approximation (Eq. 3) δmAP(B; f, D) ≈ Σ δmAP(x; f, D) is never empirically validated; impact of this approximation with correlated samples or larger batch selections remains unknown

Hyperparameter sensitivity requires detector-family tuning: 20% sampling ratio is default but Table 4 shows variance; super-batch size (80) appears arbitrary; augmentation probabilities are detector-specific (Table 10) providing limited guidance for new domains

strengths: Addresses an important, underexplored problem: online data curation for object detection with principled, metric-aware formulation rather than unstable loss signals
Rigorous mathematical foundation with closed-form expressions for efficient O(1) computation; Monte Carlo verification confirms analytical correctness

Comprehensive experimental validation across six diverse detector architectures with consistent ~+2.0 mAP gains; extensive ablations on augmentation, teacher selection, noise robustness, and KD compatibility
Practical plug-and-play design modifying only the data pipeline without architectural, loss, or optimizer changes; works across detector families and codebases
Strong robustness analysis under annotation noise (0-100%), pseudo-labels, and weaker teachers; demonstrates complementarity with knowledge distillation methods
Thorough supplementary material including rigorous proofs, Monte Carlo simulations, and additional datasets (VOC, BDD100k) validating generalization
weaknesses: Uniform prior justified primarily empirically; while ranking agreement with model-specific priors is high (ρ≈0.94), theoretical justification for maximum-entropy baseline over alternatives is limited
Significant computational overhead of 200% per-iteration wall-clock time (Table 12); dynamic scheduling mitigation reduces this by only ~30%, potentially limiting practical adoption

Strong same-family teacher requirement with notable performance drops for out-of-family teachers (Table 6), somewhat undermining 'model-agnostic' claims; unclear behavior with weaker or unavailable teachers

Unclear decomposition of improvements: Table 2 suggests strong augmentation alone slightly hurts baseline, but combined gains are substantial—contribution of DetGain vs. augmentation not fully disentangled
Limited failure analysis: no discussion of scenarios where mAP-driven selection underperforms or image types that are systematically mishandled
Evaluation scope: all experiments use ResNet-50 student models; validation with larger backbones or vision transformers absent; additional datasets relegated to appendix with single runs
First-order additive approximation validated empirically via ranking agreement (Fig. 6) but theoretical error bounds and sensitivity to |B|/|D| ratio not rigorously characterized
Data augmentation described as 'relatively naïve' with detector-family-specific tuning (Table 9); unclear how sensitive results are to augmentation strategy choices

strengths: Well-motivated problem: Clearly articulates challenges specific to detection (variable instances per image, fragmented losses, stochastic matching) that distinguish it from classification
Metric-driven approach: Using dataset-level AP rather than loss values is well-aligned with evaluation metrics and avoids instability of detection losses
Rigorous mathematical formulation: Principled derivation of marginal AP contributions with closed-form solutions and comprehensive proofs in appendix
Comprehensive experiments: Evaluates six detector architectures with multiple ablations, robustness studies (noisy labels, pseudo-labels), and additional datasets (VOC, BDD100k)
Model-agnostic design: Data pipeline modification without architectural/loss function changes enables broad applicability
Thorough supplementary material: Extensive derivations, Monte Carlo verification, and implementation details enhance technical completeness
weaknesses: Critical confound with strong augmentation: Table 2 shows DetGain alone causes overfitting (+5.7 train, -0.1 val); only the combination with strong augmentation works (+2.5). A vital ablation is missing: random 20% sampling with augmentation. Without this, the improvement may largely derive from augmentation, not DetGain itself

Unjustified uniform prior simplification: Beta(1,1) is a crude approximation of real detection score distributions. Table 10 shows model-specific Beta priors yield identical validation results (+39.6 both), undermining the necessity of the approximation. The justification of 'ordering stability' does not guarantee accurate magnitude rankings

Teacher dependency and knowledge distillation confound: Appendix 1 shows asynchronous teachers yield much weaker gains (Swin-L: +1.2 vs Res152: +2.5), contradicting 'architecture-agnostic' claims. Table 5 shows DetGain achieves comparable performance to explicit KD, making it unclear whether improvements come from data curation or implicit distillation

Modest improvements with significant overhead: Average +2.0 mAP is incremental; Table 12 shows +200% iteration time overhead. While dynamic scheduling reduces this by 30%, the cost-benefit trade-off remains unclear. Total training time impact not fully reported

Limited novelty: Core teacher-student gap directly extends RHO-LOSS [38], JEST [14], ACED [49]. Replacing loss with AP is incremental. Closed-form derivation relies on crude approximation that undermines principled appeal

Incomplete experimental validation: Limited detection-specific baselines (only Image-AP from [62]). Standard deviations in Table 1 often overlap baseline and DetGain ranges. Selection ratio k=20% not ablated; sensitivity unknown. No visualization or interpretation of which samples DetGain prioritizes

Strong augmentation is underexplored contribution: Paper describes augmentation as 'relatively naïve' yet it appears essential for success. No analysis of how much improvement comes from DetGain vs. augmentation. Missing critical ablation: uniform random 20% selection with augmentation

Overstated architecture-agnostic claims: Requires pretrained teacher and same-family architecture preference contradicts claimed generality. Asynchronous teachers show significantly degraded performance

Missing key ablations: Effect of selection ratio k unexplored; random baseline with augmentation absent; teacher training set diversity not tested; no sensitivity analysis for augmentation hyperparameters

No sample-level interpretation: Which samples does DetGain select? Are they hard examples, diverse, or high-quality? No visualization or analysis of selection patterns, failure modes, or when method underperforms

strengths: Addresses a clear gap in online data curation for object detection with well-motivated problem statement and clear articulation of why existing methods fail

Principled technical approach using AP-based marginal contributions with rigorous mathematical formulation, elegant closed-form solution (O(1) per detection), and Monte Carlo verification of analytical correctness

Comprehensive experimental validation with consistent improvements (~2.0-2.7 mAP) across 6 diverse detector architectures (Faster R-CNN, ATSS, FCOS, VFNet, GFL, Deformable DETR) demonstrating broad applicability

Strong robustness under challenging conditions: noisy annotations (maintains superiority across 0-100% noise levels), pseudo-labels (+2.8 mAP), and combines effectively with knowledge distillation (+3.7 mAP combined gains)

Fully model-agnostic design operating at data pipeline level without modifying architectures, loss functions, or training procedures; enables straightforward integration into diverse codebase implementations

Thorough ablation studies systematically examining augmentation effects (Table 2), teacher capacity impact (Table 3), prior distribution stability (Figure 4, ρ≈0.94), and comprehensive comparison with alternative metrics (Table 4)

Excellent reproducibility with clear Algorithm 1, detailed implementation specs, extensive augmentation configurations (Table 9), verified on open-source MMDetection framework, and validation on additional datasets (VOC2007, BDD100K)
weaknesses: Uniform prior (Beta(1,1)) approximation lacks complete theoretical justification—while empirical ranking stability is demonstrated (ρ≈0.94), the claim that 'absolute values are approximate but ordering is stable' is hand-wavy; gap between uniform distribution and actual detector scores not thoroughly analyzed

First-order additivity assumption (Eq. 27) only empirically validated for one regime (64→16 super-batch, Figure 6); no theoretical analysis of breakdown conditions; independence of class-level score distributions across mAP averaging not justified

Teacher-student architectural coupling significantly limits flexibility: Table 6 shows substantial performance drops with cross-family teachers (38.6 vs. 39.9 mAP), and requirement for same-family teachers with larger backbones reduces generality

Strong data augmentation emerges as hidden critical dependency: Table 2 shows pure sampling overfits severely (50.3 train vs. 37.3 val); augmentation strategy is 'relatively naïve' (authors' admission); detector-family-specific tuning (Table 9) adds hyperparameter burden

Computational overhead is substantial (3× iteration time, Table 12: 0.25s→0.75s) despite practical gains; while dynamic selection ratio (Appendix 8) recovers performance with 30% time reduction, this critical optimization is relegated to appendix and adds complexity

Limited technical novelty: core teacher-student learnability concept directly from RHO-LOSS [38] and JEST [14]; main contribution is adapting existing framework to detection via AP-based scoring—somewhat incremental; closed-form solutions under uniform prior are routine mathematics

Moderate absolute improvements (~2.0-2.7 mAP on saturated COCO benchmark) comparable to standard architectural advances rather than transformative; improvements decrease significantly with longer schedules (Table 13: 6.7 mAP at 3× vs. 2.7 at 1×), raising convergence questions

Incomplete analysis of failure modes and performance variation: 1.6-3.1 mAP range across detectors (Table 1) with no systematic explanation; no exploration of when/why DetGain underperforms; VFNet (+2.2 mAP) vs. FCOS (+2.8 mAP) discrepancy unexplained

Image-level aggregation across 80 classes and 10 IoU thresholds (800 terms in Eq. 9) assumes independence; classes and thresholds exhibit correlations; equal class weighting ignores nuanced long-tail importance despite claims of automatic mitigation

Evaluation scope limited primarily to COCO with high-capacity models (ResNet-50 students); VOC/BDD100K results relegated to appendix with single runs and no error bars; unclear performance on lightweight backbones (MobileNet, EffecientNet) or extreme long-tail distributions
